Where it began

Jeff Crowe was born in Auckland on 14 September 1958, into a family with sport in its bones. His father, Dave Crowe, turned out in three first-class games between 1953 and 1957, for Wellington and Canterbury. On his mother's side, his great-grandfather Francis Jervis was an All Black. And four years after Jeff came his brother Martin, who would also bat for New Zealand.

Jeff learned his first-class trade across the Tasman, playing for South Australia from 1977–78. There was talk that Australia might pick him, but he wanted to play for his own country, so in 1982–83 he came home to Auckland and waited to be noticed.

The player

He did not wait long. He first played Test cricket in March 1983, against Sri Lanka in Christchurch, a little over a year after Martin's, which meant the older brother had to follow the younger one in. Between 1983 and 1990 he played 39 Tests, made 1,601 runs at 26.25 with three hundreds and six fifties, and held 41 catches.

The hundred people remember came at Sabina Park in Kingston in May 1985. New Zealand were following on against a West Indies attack of Malcolm Marshall, Joel Garner and Courtney Walsh. Crowe walked out at number three with a wicket already gone and batted his way to 112. The match was lost, but the innings was one of real courage.

What made him special

Crowe was a worker. He spent long hours on his fielding, and those 41 catches were earned, not gifted; once in a while he even kept wicket. He captained New Zealand in six Tests in 1987 and 1988, and his first match in charge, in Colombo in April 1987, brought his third Test hundred, 120 not out. Of those six games, five were drawn and only one lost.

He never quite turned his promise into a long run of big scores, with three hundreds from 39 Tests. At Sabina Park, though, he showed what he could do when the bowling was at its fiercest. He also played 75 one-day internationals, including the World Cups of 1983 and 1987.

Away from the middle

Auckland gave him a benefit season in 1990–91, and he played one more summer before stopping at the end of 1991–92. He managed the New Zealand team from 1999 to 2003 and spent a spell running golf holidays in Florida.

From 2004 he became an ICC match referee, a role that took him to the World Cup finals of 2007 and 2011. He became one of the very few men to referee more than 100 Tests, and in January 2017, at the Adelaide Oval, he took charge of his 250th one-day international.

And finally

South Australia is where his first-class career began, so there was a pleasing symmetry in reaching that landmark back in Adelaide. And with an All Black, two Test cricketers and an Oscar-winning actor, his cousin Russell Crowe, in the family, Christmas conversation can rarely have run dry.
